INTERVIEW WITH JO JONES
NEA Jazz Oral History Project
Smithsonian Institution
Performing Arts
L'Enfant Plaza, Annex Building
Interviewer - Milton Hinton

This is an Exposure Production, interviewing drummer "Jo" Jonathan Jones, January 15, 1973, in New York City. My name's Milt Hinton. I'm sitting here talking with my dear friend and partner in time, the very, very great Jo Jones. It has been my pleasure to sit here and have an interview with you, Jo. I wonder if we can just really sit down and see if we can rap back and talk about some of the beautiful things about your life, so that this can be recorded for posterity so that young people and people studying about music will hear Jo Jones talk about himself and what he felt about things that he played for time immemorial.
Well, Jo, how do you feel today, Section?
I feel wonderful.

This 'Section' is that Jo Jones and I used to have a rhythm section; we're section partners. Well, Jo, what I think would be interesting to do I guess would be to start at the beginning. Where were you born, Jo?
Chicago, Illinois.
And what year was that now, about?
October 7, 1911. I believe it was on a Wednesday.
Heh-heh-heh, that's good, on a Wednesday.
Your parents' names were what, Jo?
JONES 2
Samuel and Elizabeth Jones.
Jones. Do you know about where they were living in Chicago?

At that precise time I would not and I could not possibly know; because of the nature of my father's work, which I wasn't any too familiar with, he was being shifted around in various parts of the United States and to my recollection -
Was he a railroad man?

No, he was connected with the Government and he was what is known as an artificer. In other words, aside from being an electrician, building boats and things, and you must remember the social conditions being at that particular time, it was very difficult to find an outlet for him but due to his flair of what he knew, first he was going to settle into Pittsburgh; they thought that he would go. He eventually - that's how I became to go to Alabama, you see.
How long did you stay in Chicago, I mean as a child?
I don't remember because I had a catastrophe that happened to me that I can recollect, that I was an invalid for a year and a half.
An invalid?
Yes.
How old were you?
JONES 3

I don't know; I must have been about 3, 4, or 5, 6 years old. I elected to try to copy one of my uncles lighting a cigar from a fire with a newspaper and I had a terrific burn that left me an invalid for a year and a half. I had to crawl before I could walk again and they didn't know anything about burns at that particular time. They changed two doctors at the particular time and I can remember my father bringing me silver dollars and laying them in the bed and also he brought me a ukulele. I'll never forget that. I'll always remember a ukulele; he brought me that.
Did you have any brothers or sisters, Jo?
One sister.
What was her name?
Lillian. She's living at present in New Jersey.
In New Jersey. Ann Person.

Ann Person. My sister was fortunate enough to be the first one to go into Marshall Field's, Milt, you know about Chicago, not as a domestic, because you remember/- you know how Marshall Field's felt about black people. She went in as a milliner and she went in and she also began to make hats. Then for three years she was special dietician for the Merit chain, you know, the Merit cafeteria system. She was a special dietician for them, and also/connected with Know Your City, and to be - to come from Craine University. At that particular time you know what Craine meant.
JONES
Sure, even Joe.
Yeh, you know what it meant. And remember we were going through things and meanwhile I was running and running all over the country and -

I just want to stick with the childhood over the country just for a second before you get into the cruncheon, because you mentioned a minute ago about going to Alabama, but I want to really know about how long you think you lived around Chicago before you did start to - ?

I don't remember because I told you, it was a very hectic thing. It was very hazy for me coming out of my affliction and trying to get myself together. It took me to the time I was about 16 or 17 years old to come out of this affliction.
That's interesting. So you were about the effects of 15 or 16 before you came out from under/this affliction, huh?
Of course, yes, it was a physical and not a mental thing. A The physical - thing. ..
Did you limp or anything?
No. With the scars that I bear on my body -
What part of your anatomy is it on?

My right side predominantly but I was burned from head to foot and that's an interesting story. I can remember that as though it was yesterday, how I was saved. I could not remember precisely where I was at the
JONES

particular time but I can remember all the points, as I say, as though it was yesterday and you must remember, as I explained to you, by my father being the type of man that he was, his service was requested in different places and he had to go where his service was requested for. It was beyond my mother's reach, you see, as we can know about it in the professional life. If someone wanted us in California, someone wanted us in New York, that's where we'd have to go to make our living, you see. That's in our profession and his profession at that particular time - we're coming out in an area where social conditions were very, very unique, you see, and for a black man to come into an area that he's not supposed to come into, at that particular time it was very difficult. But however due to his talent he had to be four times better than anybody else to get what he did. But he always went family. Wherever I go, my family.
I see.

But at times it was a unique situation and we didn't have the traveling situations that we have now and he could not at all times take his family. By the time he'd send his family one place, they're asking him to go somewhere else and he cannot just pick up these roots and go somewheres else until the day that he died.
Do you remember back, how long is it when your father died?
JONES 6

My father died July the 17th, 1922, and he died trying to help some college students to do something that they didn't know how to do. He was on his way to do something else and he said, "I'll show you how to do it," because they were earning their summer money so they could continue their education. And he elected to get up on a barge to try to show them how to do something and the mechanics failed in the machinery and it was like a plow, a piece of steel struck right into his back. When The lathe fell down into these great big wheels and it messed up all the machinery where these cart wheels were going, and he's on top of this barge. Everybody ducked and he ducked, but the piece of steel stuck right in his back, from the back of his neck down to the base of his spine. He was only trying to help about 20 to 30 black college students at that particular time. And It was because of him -
Where was that, Jo? What college was that?

Not the college. I know exactly where it happened. It happened in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, and that's authenticated. It is in the papers; there is a notice to that effect, July the 17th, 1922. I had went there to visit him along with my sister and I was with him on a Sunday and this occurred on a Monday. Monday, July the 17th, 1922, was definitely on a Monday. I can remember that, you see, and everybody from New Orleans on up,

anyone will tell you about my father. That's historical fact, but like I said, we could have been shifted around to Pittsburgh, we could have left Chicago, we could have wherever, and you must remember how the ship-building was, which he was the only one of his kind.
That's most interesting. What is your first recollection of your great interest in music? When did you first begin to get a feeling for music, an interest?
I had an aunt that just recently passed. She was a twin; her name was Agnes - I mean, was Mattie. This is on my mother's side of the family of about 9 children approximately.
This was Elizabeth's sister?
Yes.
What was her name?
Mattie. I always referred to her as sister Mattie because she had a twin and she took me at the time of convalescing, she took me at the time to hear the Ringling Brothers circus.
How old were you about then, Jo?
I was convalescing. I must have been about 5 or 6 or 7 years old - about 5 or 6, between 5 and 7.
This was in Chicago, right?

I don't remember. I don't know whether it was - it could have been - I'm pretty sure it was in Alabama because they sent for my father to come to work on the Warrior River and there was a Captain Baker that asked for the service of my father. Captain Baker was the kind [Black]
JONES
Monahle

of a person that later on that you heard about Fate Marlowe and all those people that worked on the Mississippi, like Captain Joe. He was Captain Baker. This was the fore-runner of a Keyser that went during World War II. He was that kind of a ship-builder but they asked for my father because my father -
Go ahead, what were you saying?
Pretty good, wouldn't you say?
Pretty good, wouldn't you say?

My father was the type of person when they had the diving suits, he didn't use a diving suit. He could go under water and stay 3 minutes without breathing. It was phenomenal. He could go on to a boat, a yacht, or what have you and he could come up without the diving suit. Those diving suits were very, very heavy. My father would just go right under the water, go in and fix up whatever happened.

So you had been to Alabama once before. This was when you were about 5 or 6 and your father died down there when you were about 16... He died in 1922, yes, that he died there, but you had made frequent trips to Alabama?

I had been traveling and traveling then. I don't know - as young as I was I could not distinguish geographically where exactly I was. But the basic things I do know because I re-traversed these places starting around after I got older to go back to try to recapitulate where was I and ask people in a town if they knew my father or if they knew what-have-you. A lot of records and things was gone.
JONES 9
So Aunt Mattie took you to the circus when you were a little boy?
I heard - I felt this bass drum. This was Mr. Emil Helmicke, the greatest bass drum player that ever lived. He was the highest paid man -
What was his name?

Helmicke, that later on played with the Goldman band up in Central Park. The last time I saw him Max Roach Art Blakey, he was 86 years old. I took ____, I took Blakey, I took Joe Harris out to hear this man play this bass drum. He was the highest priced man in the band at Central Park. The bass drum hit my stomach and I never relinquished that feeling. That was my indoctrination to music. I couldn't keep still; my aunt Mattie held me in her arms. That's when she went and bought me a drum.

What I would like to do is things that I - have about three sections of articles and things - I've thrown away a lot of things and I dedicated in from the very beginning to what I would do. I wrote a thing in the articles and things that I have that hasn't been published, "Peoples I've Met". I cover the 48 states and I would like to make a jump from where we are now to start in the year 1930, which would be important.

We got lot's of time to do that, Jo, and it's important - one of the stipulations that I have in the interview is that (I can read it to you) you should get the background, you know, the early background, so that after I work into that with you I'm just going to let
JONES 10
you talk about whatever you want to talk about.

...You must remember this, Milt, that all the books that have ever been written about various musicians, they start with me, I joined Count Basie in 1935. He joined Count Basie in 1936. That sounds like I was just born, like Topsy. But what about the years from '26 to '36?
That's what we're trying to cover now.
This's where we're getting to. From the year '26 we go professionally - and I can start with you very vividly -
(TELEPHONE RINGS)

...Let me get this... Sitting here talking to you is a very - I don't know how to express these vibrations, but I'm sure on the tape the telephone which I would like to always remain in this tape, rang a couple of times and we stopped the tape just to answer the phone; the first time it was an old buddy who was in the Basie Band, Earl Warren, calling. Very spiritual. Then behind that Claude Hopkins, the great piano player of our era -
That was spiritual.
...Then I said I believe I better call and check with Roy Eldridge and I called and spoke to Roy. Before we hung up -
More spiritual.
Before Roy could get off the phone the other phone rang and who was it but Buddy Rich...
Traps...These are things that nobody, the three
JONES 11

and a fourth billion peoples of the world will not know, how small the world is with an airplane and a telephone, how could you and I be sitting here 'way away from everybody and all these things come into place?
Buddy Rich was calling from Florida...
And I asked him about his father. His father is in his eighties... because I've only known Buddy since he was 6 years old.
Right. Now we want to get back to you, but I thought we should mention that as a sort of a spiritual vibration thing -
Of course, that's the way music operates.

- that seems to generate with you and certainly when I'm around you it seems to envelop me too. Now getting back to where you were talking about where you were and the great sensation that took over your whole being when your aunt took you to hear the Ringling Brothers Circus band and the bass drum Emil Helmicke played. I just want to ask you, where did you get your first set and what was it like? How did you get into that?

Well, with a series of things but I remember that my aunt bought me this snare drum and I was trying to do other things and everybody in the neighborhood, the kids, in the various one of the last neighborhoods I stayed in, they had come out to play just the snare drum. And throughout that later on in life there was a fellow by the name of Bill Taft Jordan. I remember very well, it can come to me now
JONES 12

that when I was in Birmingham, Alabama, living in Esley Heights and I passed by a florist's by the name of Kelly Florists.. I knew a candlemaker by the name of Mr. Blackburn - that all these people had to do something with me making my life, because during that period I was very fortunate to meet peoples like Rudolph Valentino, Mr. Jack Dempsey, Judge Ebel Gary that Gary, Indiana, was named after him.
Was this when you were a kid?

That's right, I was a kid and I know good and well my recollections of Birmingham, Alabama, was they had a school called Tuggle Institute and they had a fire. I remember I saw it and I thought it was a blast furnace from the TCI works, but it wasn't. I looked at where I was staying and it was the Tuggle Institute where... Grimes, Hunch Grimes there was and that's where peoples had played. This woman was a very educator and it was a black school where underprivileged children could go and peoples -
Did you go to that school?

Yes, I did, because of the peoples that had migrated to the South that went into the coal and iron industry from up North. They, from a social standpoint point of view, they helped the poor people. They had a cook, maid, butler, or chauffeur, they had a child they sent the child to Tuggle Institute and that was before what we know as write-offs now. That was theirs. It was a forerunner of the Community Chest at that particular time. When I come out of there I was going to play trumpet. A fellow named George Hudson
JONES
was teaching me how to play trumpet.
This was in Alabama?

In Tuggle Institute. George Hudson that later went into St. Louis and he's still in St. Louis and he played with Jeter-Pillars. Later on after I grew up I played in the band with him. He's in St. Louis as of now, as far as I know, and I started on the trumpet and I tried to play the sax and I tried to play the piano. I didn't know what I was going to do, and - and throughout that my talent of going with the dancing and the singing and what have you, then all these peoples I met. At that particular time - there was a fellow at Tuggle Institute by the name of Walter Young, that went from Tuggle Institute on the trumpet and went to Switzerland. Those records stand. His name was Walter Young. Then after that there was a fellow by the name of Hunch Grimes, you see, and that was my infancy but my outlet to run into an Edgar Battle that later on became the bandleader for the great Jack Hoxey show, the first time that a black man could stay in a white hotel in Birmingham and Mobile and Nashville and Chattanooga. Edgar Battle did not go into no back doors because they didn't know nothing about racial discrimination because they respected the man because he was the bandleader and nobody knows that Edgar Battle, coming out like (Walter B. Crill) and - Lord, you had the John Phillip Sousa Band but who did you have - you had P. G. Lowry that played on the side

of the band, but nobody had ever led. Jack Hoxey was a terrific cowboy like the Tom Mix here. But he had the One-O-One Ranch and who was the head bandmaster was Edgar Battle, a black man, not a white man. This was something that the Jet, Ebony, and the Pittsburgh Courier and nobody ever wrote about, because he only got - when he got to New Orleans he got writeups in the Picayune. When he got to Cincinnati it was the Cincinnati Inquirer. They said Edgar Battle; they didn't say black man. They said Edgar Battle. Edgar Battle stayed in all premier hotels before the advent of Civil Rights. Here I am and I was running around and I was going to Switzerland to go with Walter Young as a small unit but I wasn't allowed to go. I deviated myself to some ways and somehow or other I wound up at the A and M Institute in Huntsville, Alabama. Right on the outskirts 4 miles away is a place called Normal, Alabama, and at that time there was one of the greatest, foremost cornetists in the whole world. His name was James H. Wilson, because (who) Walter Crill worked on the Chautauqua shows was supposed to be America's foremost cornetist but Mr. James H. Wilson was the only one that could play the cadenza of a tune called "Salute Polka" and "Nelly Bly" also. He was the only one. That's when I began to get my musical education. I used to go -
You played with these gentlemen?

Of course I played with Mr. Wilson but however when I went into the band room and he put up "Poet and Peasant" it took me two months to get back into the room. I didn't know nothing about a half note or less.
That was in Huntsville, right?
JONES 15

Normal, Alabama, N-o-r-m-a-l. See because right out from that was the Seventh Day Adventists that later on a lot of peoples joined that. It's Huntsville, J.F. Drake, Alabama, they say, and later on Professor Jack (Tfadrick?) became the Professor. But Mr. James H. Wilson, he had been with the 24th and he had been with the 10th Cavalry and he was a flexible man. He was the one that told me about Louis Armstrong; but here's a man that's playing classical music, what does he know about Louis Armstrong? I knew about Charlie Charleston; I knew about Johnny Dunn but I -
Who was Charlie Charleston?

Charlie Charleston played with a band out of Jackson, Tennessee, and he was born originally in St. Louis and I thought that he was the man and Johnny Dunn, but Mr. Wilson told me this is no, Louis Armstrong. I said, who is Louis Armstrong? So I had a distant cousin that took me back in Chicago and I went to see Mr. Louis Armstrong playing with Erskine Tate at the Vendome Theatre with that trumpet with the spotlight on him - I quickly gave up the trumpet. I thought I was going to play saxophone and later on in my years, in my formative years, having as a kid, dabbled around in shows, in Chautauqua shows, in carnivals and circuses and little gilly shows and what have you, I was in an advantage to travel. Then I was going to play
JONES

saxophone and here comes Coleman Hawkins, so forget it, so I switched to the piano. In 1930 Adelaide Hall came to Omaha, Nebraska. By that time I had migrated because I was going to continue my education, I thought, because I was with a band at the time called Skeet Morgan and R. C. Hicks and their Dixie Ramblers. We found ourselves out at Chillicothe, Missouri -
What were you playing at that time? Were you playing drums then?
I was playing drums.
This was around 1930?

Yes. But I wasn't quite sure whether I played drums or piano because sometimes you'd catch me, I would be playing saxophone. Sometimes I'd be singing. Some places I'd be dancing. Some places I'd get on the show, I'd be doing everything because I remember in 1930 I joined a show and there were 3 pianists. A piano player by the name of Troy and Floyd; Washington, was his last name. That's all I knew because they only called him Washington because in those days they only called, Washington. Meanwhile I had had the fortune of meeting the guys that made the QRS Little records, the fellows like Lou Louis. I have been fortunate enough to have met Seminole because I was moving all the time and what was so fortunate -
Were you on your own now or were you still -
I was on my own, because in those days, Milt, you know good and well that when you joined a show
JONES

had to be you were recommended from your minister or your rabbi or somebody and you had to be 25 years old before you drank alcohol. You just didn't come out and say, I'm 18, I'm eligible to drink. You didn't go into no nightclub. But at the same time, that way we were juveniles and you started in show business young. You had a whole lot of fathers and uncles and mothers out here, you see, and what was so remarkable about it, they taught us moral and civic discipline. Because you remember at that time the Billboard had a thing called the blacklist. If you picked up that issue and saw your name on the blacklist, that meant that you was grounded for a year. It was impossible for you to get on a (Sells-Floto) it was impossible for you to get on a Ethel Waters or a Ma Rainey or a Whitman Sisters show. It was impossible for you to get a job shining shoes on the Sahara Desert.
End of side 1, tape I.

You just mentioned Ethel Waters and Ma Rainey had a show. These were black shows... We just want it for the records so that the reader and the listener will know that these were great shows - and the Whitman Sisters -

I met in 1923, I met Butterbeans and Suzie and I was running errands and getting their food at the Frolic Theatre in Birmingham, Alabama. That's authenticated and truthfully. Everything that is really in show business, and Miller and Lyles and all that.
JONES 18

It's no way in the world that Eddie Lemons and his Dashing Dinah Revue show - these people had cars, they had 7 or 8 cars on the railroad that had their names on it. That was a big black act. Miss Ida Cox, which she was on a recording, when she came in she still had her diamonds and only had about 80 homes in Knoxville.
Hey, you and I made that record.
We did with Coleman Hawkins and Roy Eldridge.
We want to pull that out and we'll take an intermission.
With Roy Eldridge and Sammy Price.
We should play that.

And she still had the same authentic diamonds that she always had. They didn't find her washing dishes at Macy's. And Butterbeans and Susie, when they bought their home in Chicago anyone could come to that, anyone who was in the profession. When Miss Ethel Waters, before she went into "As Thousands Cheer" to tour all over, when she came out with the great bandleader Leroy Smith, when she had that show she didn't have no money -
That was a black band.
Leroy Smith, as far as I know he was an eastern black.
Buffalo, New York.
Because I only got a chance to see it once.
*Eddie Lemons' troupe originated in Cincinnati.
JONES 19

It came through Omaha in the thirties. Speaking about Roy Eldridge, when I saw Mr. Roy Eldridge - incidentally, he started on drums and I started on trumpet. I came out with the then Erskine Hawkins. Erskine Hawkins didn't go where I went; he went to Dozier Park.
Did you ever play with Erskine Hawkins' band?

Of course not, because when you look up and see Erskine, Erskine would be on trumpet and I would be on trumpet. Until 1930 I was playing the second part to 'Beau Koo Jack.' Of course I had to put a Coca-Cola bottle... 'Beau Koo Jack' in the key of B flat. Mr. Don Redman (HUMS) - that's on the second page and you paid 50¢ for that stack. That was a big stack. 'Beau Koo Jack' and 'Louisiana Bobo.' See I played all those things... But my embouchure went away because at the same time I had met a fellow by the name of Kid Lips Hackett and Kid Lips was a sensational drummer, but also he was a prizefighter and when the shows that he was on couldn't make their money he'd go down to the auditorium or the YMCA and get on and pick up a 20 or 25 dollars and come back to feed people, because shows would get stranded. So I was going to be a prizefighter. So there went my embouchure. But without my embouchure about losing embouchure, when I saw Mr. Louis Armstrong playing with Erskine Tate down in the theater playing his thing, I quickly gave that up! But when I made the most fatal
JONES 20

mistake in my life, as I tried to tell you, is when Adelaide Hall came to Omaha, Nebraska; Joe Turner on the piano; Art Tatum on the piano. She had three pianists. You must remember in these areas the only way a black person beside Dan and Eddie which were European that worked - they were two black men that worked in tuxedos - when you played the RKO or the Keith's circuit or the Pantages circuit, you had to put on a bandanna, you see. There had to be a cotton scene. But these people came over with class. Here's a woman, Adelaide Hall, came up with 3 pianists. Joe Turner, Art Tatum, and the other pianist - I'll have to go to Europe and try to find out this guy's name. I should know him but - but these are the only two people impressed me in the . But I felt sorry for Art Tatum and since I went to work at 11 o'clock on my piano job, because at this time I would switch from the piano to the drum -
This was in Omaha? Around 1930?

In Omaha. When I found a piano player that was limpid, I'd go and push him off the job. But here comes some hobo would push me off the job. So I'd go around the corner and find me a weak drummer and push him off the job. And here would come another drummer would push me off the job. The greatest drummer that ever lived in the whole world that made me what I am today is a fellow
JONES

by the name of Manzie Campbell. I forgot that I met Mr. Manzie Campbell with the Collier Shows; the greatest show that you had that toured nowhere but in the South was Mr. Collier's Show. Mr. Collier had two daughters who was very light-skinned and they said, "Limabeans from New Orleans." But that wasn't the name of the show... which you know the name of the show...
What was this gentleman Mancy like?

Manzie Campbell was the only man that I have ever seen or met, or anybody ever met in the world, that could take his left hand and play a perfect drum roll. The show that he was on - I had met him - was a silent screen show. You must remember in those days when P. G. Lowry was playing the side show - this was before the Ubangi tribe because the only attraction they had was Eko and Iko. They were two albinos that when one would say one thing, the other would repeat. "How's the weather today?" "How's the weather today?" "It's going to rain today." "It's going to rain today." And that was a 25¢ addition to the side show.
Meanwhile there was a black man that looked exactly like Jack Johnson. He was from Oklahoma. His name was Crack Johnson. Crack Johnson played in the big tent with John Philip Sousa.
What did he play?
Drums.
He played where?
JONES 22
With John Philip Sousa. They had him in the big show, under the big tent.
What show was this?

Ringling Brothers, Barnum and Bailey and whatever you read about Ringling Brothers, Barnum and Bailey they have to have crack Johnson there in his picture, a black man. He looked like Jack Johnson. But the drummer I spoke about, nobody in the whole world has ever played that much drums, because I forgot that I had met the man and years later I did a faux pas. I made a boo-boo. I did something wrong and this man came several years later and sat down at the drums where I was playing and he said, 'Son, you might go far. Don't make that mistake no more.' And he told me how to learn how to play drums, because I was trying to emulate the popular drummers in the territory that I was in, because as far as I was concerned, this was my world. I wasn't going nowhere. When I got to Omaha, Nebraska, I had made it. I wasn't going to go nowhere. Now I have met peoples that have traveled the whole world. They've been over to Europe, Australia, they've been everywhere and they tried to tell me, but I knew. I was smarter than they were. Don't tell me nothing; I'm Chicken Little; and this man, Monzie Campbell, the greatest drummer that ever lived, any way you wanted it, because it come to my mind I saw him but I didn't realize
JONES
what he was doing.
Who was he with, Jo, Mancy Campbell?

He was with Collier's Shows and it was impossible, see, 'cause he had people like Johnny Hudgins on that show. You couldn't get on that show. That was the greatest show and they never came up North. That was Collier and his two daughters. a different thing... ^ It was only in later years that they extended up through Canada, but I mean Mr. Collier had died, you see, and all those peoples, all those big peoples in there - Willie Too Sweet and all those peoples - and Johnny Knox who was one of the greatest comedians that ever lived - the only one that I'd ever compare with him - Johnny Knox was out of Detroit - John Mason was the natural. Everybody knew he was a natural; and nobody knew about Pigmeat. I knew Pigmeat when he was on carnivals and HINTON: Pigmeat Markham. JONES: nobody ever saw Pigmeat in New York, like They would see him in Philadelphia when he'd get in front of a chorus line. He would take on a chorus where the chorus girl was supposed to take the thing, you see. But back to the music -
When did you begin to get with dance bands and bands other than out of the circus?... Were there any bands that you begin to now get into like dance bands or what we consider orchestras now?
Milt, I was fortunate enough - I didn't think that I'd ever take music as a vocation. I didn't think that I'd ever take music as whatever; because as I told you
JONES 24

at the time I had something handed down to me. I was going to be a surgeon and I was going to Switzerland. That's the reason when I was about 16 I was going to go to Switzerland. But I was playing with a piano player and my mother said, "Well, if Calvin don't go, you can't go." I was going with Walter Young.
Who's Calvin?
A piano player, just a piano player.
Your mother knew him well?
Yes, he took me on as a kid.
When you played with him, you played drums, huh? Like a piano and drum combo. I just wanted to make it clear for the record.

During those periods in different parts and places I've been and always running around, when the show gets stranded in what area - Chattanooga, Louisville, Paducah, or what area - they'd come over and ask me from those roadhouses, you come over and play in this band. I was integrating then. They knew me as Jo. I'd come in and play with these bands. I didn't know nothing about white and colored. I just thought it was music, just so nobody don't bother my drums, I knew where I'd stand.
