for two weeks. They went to Boston; J. C. played with the band 9 days and left. They came to me and said, "Where can I find a drummer?" I got Gus Johnson because I knew Gus and I knew Gus had tried to play bass. I mean, he was a musician and he knew all about it. I said, "Well, you can play in there." I went down to Nol Studio and rehearsed the band. I said, "You got the job." And Gus stayed there till Basie's band broke up, you know, '50 or '51.
Then he went with a small band.
With a small group.
...Wardell Gray and Buddy DeFranco...
Yes, Buddy DeFranco and the bass player that played with tape on his hand - Jimmy Lewis, and Freddie Green. Freddie Green was playing with Lester Young at the Birdland, and Joe Shulman -
Joe Shulman, a very good bass player. He used to play with Claude Thornhill. A dear friend of mine, a magnificent bass player.

Joe Shulman took his whole salary and gave it to Freddie Green. Basie came down, and Morris Levy will tell you, Morris Levy was paying at an unheard salary of $125 a week. The scale was $87. The man from the union - they had moved the union on 52nd Street - and the man came in and told Morris Levy that he was paying too much money. Morris Levy says, "I'm not paying enough. You're from the
JONES 197

union; can I pay these people more?" Then I stayed there with Billy Taylor, John Collins, Lloyd Troutman. They built the Embers because of Billy but they kept Billy at the Down Beat, sent Billy over there with streamers on... break

Just take a break and relax for a bit. Hey, Jo, I'm going to play some Teddy Wilson, Jo Jones, and Milt Hinton. Can't remember what year we did this in but we were doing a television show at CBS called "On a Saturday Afternoon", called the Teddy Wilson Hour and then we made an album with it for Norman Granz. Let's listen to some of that.
(MUSIC)
That was beautiful. That was the first side of that Teddy Wilson, Jo Jones, and Milt Hinton. When did we make that, Jo, I've forgotten?
It was in the 50's.

Jo, just as a record, we've been spending a good deal of time here, the few times we've been here. Now it's January 29th, 1973. We're still going on this thing but we're up to the 50's. You said those records made with Teddy Wilson were about in the 50's, huh?
The 50's, coming into the 60's.
So what did you do after - I remember we stayed in the Embers there till practically they closed it. I went with somebody to go some place. Joe Bushkin left.
JONES 198
I remember we stayed in the Embers there for a while with Joe Bushkin.

You know you went up and down the Street for one year, one block one year. I did a little house there with Dorothy Donegan and Joe Bushkin and Tyree Glenn. Of course, I had the trio there with Hank Jones, my original trio with Hank Jones, Tommy Potter -
(TELEPHONE RINGS)

... We got up to about the 50's. We got up to 54th Street with us working. I worked with you and Joe Bushkin and Buck Clayton and Stuff Smith at the Embers and then we all went our separate ways. You stayed there with your own trio...
I had Hank Jones, Tommy Potter, and myself.
Didn't you start with Don Abney when Joe Bushkin left?
No, Hank Jones, Tommy Potter, and myself. Don Abney only played the dinner hour.
Joe Bushkin left now?
Joe Bushkin had gone...
I stayed there; I was supposed to stay there.
But you went up the street.
Tommy Potter came in.
Tommy came in and I got Hank Jones.
Before Tommy came in, when the trio started
JONES 199
with Tyree, for several nights it was Don Abney -

No, Don Abney played the dinner hour. He played up till 9 o'clock by himself. I had the trio. Tyree was doing the Ted Steele show and we thought - Barbara Carroll had been in there and Joe Shulman, who later married her. Then we decided - and Ralph Watkins said, "This would be good." It was a Jo Jones trio featuring Tyree Glenn. We came in for one week and we stayed 17 weeks. Then the next time we came back in for 16 weeks, it was Tyree Glenn's quartet with the same people and we only changed the uniform, because I went down to Tie City and bought dollar and a half ties. It was the same people there. We did 17 weeks; we did 16 weeks; and meanwhile Tyree was still doing the Ted Steele show on WPIX. Later on... Tiny Kahn had died and Tyree says, "Why don't you take the job?"
Tiny Kahn was a very good drummer.

You better believe. He was one of my children like the other children. I said, "You take it. I'm not going to get up at that time in the morning." Because you remember at the same time I was doing the thing with the Teddy Wilson show that you and I used to do every Saturday.
CBS, yes.
That's right, CBS. I said, no, I won't be able to do that because to come out of the Embers and then

to stay up to do that morning show, I'd need so much time and in rest, because at that time I was out here by myself and I had nobody to help me until I got - well, Specs was stuck in a studio and then later on - that's where, at the time, don't you remember that we were doing things, and of course you left Fess and I got Osie and I said, "Osie, you'll have to do these things."
Fess is Cab Calloway. So after that where did you go? Now we're up to the 60's. We made a tour, by the way; we forgot to mention that.
When we did the 5 or 6 weeks with the Jackie Gleason show with Joe Bushkin, you, Buck Clayton, and myself, and Zuma Cunningham who was responsible for taking Mr. Clark Gable to Hollywood.
A great lady and a good actress.
The first one, when he did The Honeymooners -
The lady who tried the shoes on.
We went through all that and we had the DeMarco Sisters, and there was Art Carney.
That was a great tour, wasn't it?

Of course it was. That's when I found out that Jackie Gleason was the Fatty Arbuckle of his time because - he was a well-read man and he had the children. But this particular tour that we did was very remarkable. Now we go back after that -
How long was that tour, Jo?
JONES
The tour lasted 5½ or 6 weeks.
Let's name some of the towns. We went first to Pittsburgh.
Pittsburgh; we went to Detroit. We played Chicago at the Chicago Theatre.
Youngstown, Akron, Cincinnati -
We played Cincinnati. We played all of them.
Boston. I think the tour closed in Boston.

We closed in Boston because at the time, I think it was June or July, because I have a record that when I came into the Birdland with Tony Bennett and some more peoples and I was supposed to play with Basie's band at that particular time, I sat in the audience and I did not play in the band because I had to leave.
We had such a ball! The DeMarco Sisters - what was that guy's name, Stan something, a very funny guy -

A comedian that did all the parts. Then you remember that Jackie would always say, "Milt, didn't you fix the coffee?" and if he didn't get that coffee, that was it. Jackie at that particular time had a weight problem.
He contributed a great deal to jazz, didn't he?
One of the great supporters of jazz.

Oh, please. You remember the thing we did in Detroit? I went out and got Tommy Gamble - that's when we got Ahmad Jamal to come into the Embassy. There was about a party of 23 was down there. Jackie had the Presidential Suite at the Book-Cadillac. We said, well, we'll just go
JONES 202
around the corner and get some barbecue. Jackie said, "I've got $300 worth of barbecue! And his weight went up and naturally when we went to....
Tommy Gamble's house. He was one of the great sportsmen of Detroit, Tommy Gamble. Jackie was such a great supporter of jazz, wasn't he?

Yes. After that Jackie had the trumpet player that we all know so well to sit down just to make one record just for personal people and he only wanted to send this record out. Do you remember when we went to the Parke-Sheraton and Jackie was in the deep freeze, talking about he had to sober up. He put everything out of there. We were upstairs trying to figure out what we were going to play on the show. Buck had gone somewhere, and he did "Bob-a-loo" and he got Bobbie and he only did this record just for a few friends. Because, as I said, you know we know that he's well read, but out of that we did a thing. But at the time, you must remember, Milt, that you, Buck, Joe Bushkin, or myself were in demand and everybody was pulling on us. They didn't allow us the chance to be, to do what we wanted to do. However, out of that we did a lot of things.
A lot of very nice things, very happy things. So now we're in the 60's. What did you do in the 60's?
You know I always was still connected with
JONES 203
Norman Granz. I was always connected with the Newport Festival.
We did the first Newport Festival, didn't we, Jo?
Of course.
Do you remember who we played for? You were the house drummer, of course. You played with everybody.
Well, I had my drums there and it was raining. It started raining at 8 o'clock. Gene Krupa had to play on my drums. We played at the casino.....
You, Teddy Wilson, and I played for Billie Holiday, at the first Newport Jazz Festival. We played for Billie Holiday.
At the very first, and they only wanted it for one year because they were trying to break down the status quo of the social people...
They gave big parties for us.

Pearl Mesta was there. I stayed down at the Lorillards Buena Vista. Van Allen was there. I.... we went down to the party and everything like that. But you were there. You were playing; Buck Clayton was playing. Lester Young was there. Billie Holiday was there, you see.

Ray Brown was there. I remember flying up first Festival that was the very there with Teddy Wilson in a small plane... I can't remember what year that was in, but we were there. It's a matter of record.
JONES 204
So now then, '65, this is up to '70. You've been going back and forth to Europe.

You must remember, I came through Canada and Ray Bryant was playing with Carmen McCrae. I said, "You're fired." So I formed a trio for one year. I had it for 11 1/2 months. I had Ray Bryant and his brother and I said, now this is it. Then after I did that, then I left and I went to San Juan to open up Ochos Puertos, Hinton: Ochos Puertos. Eight Doors. There was a laundry there. It was one block from the Governor's mansion in old San Juan. I was in Pepi Alegria and I had a partner that understood about musicians and tried to do this thing and we did this. Ray Bryant and his brother Tommy went on with their own trios in which they are as of today. Ray has his own trio.

One of the finest records I think I've ever heard of a trio, and one of the best recorded drum albums I've ever heard in my life, is the one that you made with Ray Bryant and his brother Tommy Bryant and you, called Jo Jones Plus Two.
We didn't know what we was doing... so we just sat down and played naturally.

Well of all the records that I've missed playing on here, I have a few tracks of these and I'd like to - at the end of this I'll put a few tracks of these on so it is a matter of history that people will know about these, because never have I ever had anybody play as
magnificently as you played on those.
I didn't play, Milt. All I was doing was sitting there listening. It was things like what I did with you or what I did with Teddy. I was always an audience. I will be an audience as long as I live.
How do you mean that, Jo?

It's very difficult to teach people how to play with people, not for people. Because to be able to sit up on the bandstand and play with the people that you play with and sit and listen - the drum is a very unique instrument since it is the first. You sit and listen to learn how to play with people before you play for people. It's an automatic thing if you're going to play for an audience, you got people out there. You know I told you a long time ago I didn't know nothing about the drum. I had to learn how to play the drum from Mr. Walter Page. Without the bass fiddle I don't know how to play. The bass is the foundation. That's the reason I always refer to you as 'Section.' That's the reason I ask you. I'm not asking from the trumpet player, the saxophone player, the trombone player, the violin player - I have to ask you where I'm going. You and I both have been fortunate enough to play around peoples that lived in a certain way that we can do this thing. Somehow coming out of what you're talking about, it's very difficult to explain how
JONES 206
that Buck Clayton, Milt Hinton, Joe Bushkin, and myself can sit down tonight and play as though we just played yesterday.
Music is just that close, yes. We understand each other. Our lives are intermingled... with our music

That's the word, that's the keyword is understanding. Learn how to play with people, not for people. We were very fortunate. It's impossible, and we would love to impart this to the youngsters, to learn how to play with people, nqt just sit at home and listen to the records or read the: write-ups, just to learn how to play with peoples.
(BREAK)
Now, you've been down to Puerto Rico and you did the Eight Doors.
Paul Nevers on the piano, and a bass player because of bringing that you know so much and so well.../Juan Tizol up to New York. Escudero ... [Bob Escudero]
Did he play bass in Puerto Rico?
He played in the trio that I opened up with. /There's another great Puerto Rican musician that's down there, a trombone player.
Oh, Arbello. He's with Don Redman, oh yes, of course. (Fernando Arbello, trombonist)
One of the most authentic jazz men in all of jazz right now in 1973 is - I certainly hope everybody will get
down there and research him because his world of knowledge is absolutely invaluable. That's the very great Garvan Bushell.
HINTON: Garvin.

was the cause of Coleman Hawkins [St. Joseph] first leaving his home in St. Joe, Missouri. Milt, there's something that very few people know. Coleman Hawkins had a ring and I had a ring, and I still have it. His mother and my mother in Omaha, Nebraska, Mrs. Louise Kelly, were friends.
Who's Mrs. Louise Kelly, your mother?
That's right.
What is Garvin's mother's name, do you know?
North. But I was speaking about Garvin.
The only way he could leave to go up on the show - he was like a godfather of Coleman Hawkins. His mother wasn't going to let him leave to go and Bushell took him. He's alive today.
Jerry Jerome just came back from there and told me
He's got a big trio down there... He's got a group that sounds just marvelous.

He hangs out with Pablo Casals and he still do the things, you see. But this is a man that's on his third life. We knew, we found out that later on in life that I met this man and he knew about Mr. Coleman Hawkins - but Garvan Bushell was the first one to bring Coleman Hawkins out into the world.
JONES 208
Let's get back to you, Jo, now. What did you do in '65, can you recall?
I was still around recording and doing things, but I was still with the Jazz Philharmonic -
Your usual trips. Did you make a yearly trip to Europe, is that so?
At that particular time, sure.
You still do, don't you?
Yes, as of now I am.
The last few years you've made trips to Europe. Who do you go there with?

Well, from 1969 I started out with Milt Buckner, an organist, a drifting organist and pianist. I did things with him with piano and things like that. We took the dancers over and we did this and we did that.
What dancers, Jo?
We had Baby Lawrence. We had Jimmy Slide.
This is a group of tap dancers?
Tap dancers, yes. Europe had never seen these kind of dancers before. We did things throughout Germany, throughout Spain, throughout France. It was a most gratifying thing. It was very wonderful.
I remember that year before last, I think it was, Hugues Panassie's son, Hugues Panassio the great jazz impresario who lives in France and has contributed a great

deal to jazz - his son came over here and did a movie. It was like a discography of jazz. He got you, he got Buck Clayton. I did some with him. He did some with you in Europe. Then he came over here and did something with Jimmy Crawford.
That's right, 'jazz and all that,' which is a movie that's all the way in Europe.
I saw some of the movies he did of you and Milt Buckner in France and they were just amazing and I haven't seen anything like that here in the United States.

What Louis Panassie in France to do with this thing - he would like to come over to take it out to the colleges himself. He don't want to give it to nobody else because he wants it to be for educational purposes. He's going to do that. Other people would love to get it. I mean the networks such as CBS, NBC - they'd love to get it but he will not give it to them because he don't want it like that, because he's trying to do something in regards to his father, Hugues Panassie. I just got through doing the thing with Jimmy Slide and he did a whole thing that's in the movie that Mr. Duke Ellington's whole entire band is on the thing. This thing is going to be coming out to go around to all the colleges of the United States. It's an educational thing. Right now it is in Europe; it is in France, in Spain, in Germany and what have you.
JONES 210
I saw one of the most wonderful things of you, about 15 minutes of drum solos by you, in some little small club over there and it was just absolutely beautiful.
Oh, this was horrible. It was in -
It was horrible? I thought it was beautiful.
Yes, because I didn't know it was a movie. I was going out to play tennis and I went down and I had on a shirt -
Do you still play tennis, Jo?
Yes. So I went down and I said, 'What are you doing?' They got the cameras and all this. We were in Biarritz. That's right on the border of the south of France, before you go into Spain.
What are you doing now, right now? This is 1973 and in the next 3 or 4 days I think you were getting ready to go back.
I had planned to join Milt Buckner in Europe.
Have you got any particular place to start?

Just a second, Jo. (SOUND OF TAPE RUNNING OUT) It was 1972. We were all up at Yale University for the Duke Ellington Yale Fellowship, about 30 or 40 jazz musicians, of which I most graciously appreciate being considered one of. You certainly were there. The drummers consisted of Jo Jones, Max Roach, Kenny Clarke -
That was flown all the way from Paris, France.
JONES 211
Who else?
little Tony Williams.

Tony Williams was a guest. There was another drummer there, I can't remember now, But you were there and it was a glorious three days. We played and had these jam sessions with Mary Lou Williams and with the great Duke Ellington's orchestra. You want to say something about that, Jo?

The young man was there, naturally, Mr. Eubie Blake and his partner Mr. Noble Sissle. However, they elected me to take care of Eubie Blake, Duke Ellington, and what have you. They told me that I had to take the children into hand. You remember all the bass players was there - Charlie Mingus, George Duvivier, Ray Brown, Sam Stewart... all you guys were there. But they turned it over to me, says, "Will you take care of these little teenagers." And I was trying to make like I was 22 years old. What happened was that I wind up hanging out with Mr. Eubie Blake, who was the youngest man in the whole conglomeration. He was younger than Duke Ellington, he was younger than Willie the Lion, he was younger than everybody else. You must remember that I wasn't supposed to speak anything when we went out to get our plaque, but I did have to say what I had to say and that's a matter of record.
It's a matter of record, Jo, but there was a great thing that you did there that was so marvelous.
JONES 212

The mere fact that you were there was a marvelous thing, and Mr. Eubie Blake, who was just as effervescent as anyone could possibly be. I don't think we mentioned - especially with the big bass players I got to try to mention every one of them because I would never want it said that I didn't mention all of the bass players. There was Charlie Ming s. There was Ray Brown. There was George Duvivier. There was Slam Stewart; and Mr. Ruff which produced the whole thing, and yours truly, so I think I did cover it.

...You remember, Milt, you and I made a record and I always had in my heart that I was going to make a record with 5 bass players. I always said I was going to have Richard Davis; I always said I was going to have George Duvivier; I always said I was going to have Ray Brown... And I went on down the line. But when we sat in the back room, I said, "Now I got all you people here and I'll go out here with my drum and I'll kill all you people... At last after 4 or 5 years I got all you people together. You must remember that out of the things that we did, Milt, that you were the coordinator to get what you have now going with the bass thing."
Oh, we have a wonderful bass choir. We have a very beautiful bass choir and I'm very proud of it.
Milt, it's impossible, not improbable - it's impossible, it's improbable for, as I reiterated before,
long before this, there's no way in the world that a man playing in the percussion section if he sit down with a drum, he don't know how to play with the bass fiddle. It's lost.
Well, we have to all play together...

That's what I mean. Now once he plays with the bass fiddle it's like the heart, the lungs of the body, and then he goes and he plays. But the most gratifying thing, as we were speaking about the Yale thing, it was the greatest thing that personally I have ever had a chance to see, that I'm sitting up on the bandstand. I didn't get a chance to play with you. I was playing with Duke Ellington, Harry Edison, and I played with Ray Brown. Ray Brown says, 'What am I playing?' And I said, 'Don't ask me; ask Duke Ellington.' I'm mad because I don't get a chance to play with you or George Duvivier. You and George Duvivier made me quit recording because I didn't have you to play on the bass. It's like they used to do with the Brooklyn Dodgers. 'Who's on first? Gil Hodges.' I said, 'Do you mean to tell me - who have you got playing bass with me?' I would not show up. Everybody thought that I had a whole lot of money; but they didn't understand that it's impossible for me to play, because, Milt, you must remember this - the foundation of this whole thing that we have - let's go back to the classics - you start with the tympani and the bass.
They start from the bottom. Peoples like you or Charlie Mingus or Ray Brown or what have you, you are the basics of the academy of the music field.

Coming from you, Jo, thank you. But let's get on with you now because this is so very important, because this is your day and we want these young people, whoever would search out, to know about you and the great things that you've tried to do in the whole taking of this thing. So now we're up to 1972. Here it is 1973 -
And I'm fixing to go to Europe in a few minutes, after I get through talking to you. I'm supposed to join Milt Buckner.
How long will you be over, Jo?
Oh, about 6 weeks, give or take.

I'm going to miss you. But before you leave we're going to have one more record date. This is Monday. We're going to have a record date Wednesday with the great George Barnes and the great Rube Brown is going to be on that date. JONES: Well, that'll be all right. Who's the piano, Hank Jones and whoever, I don't remember now, but it's going to be a great session. We're looking forward to doing this thing. Harry Lim which is going to produce it, which is a great responsibility. Was that Keynote Jazz many years ago?
Yes, you see, because we must remember, Milt, that we were going through a lot of social changes at the
JONES 215
period when Harry Lim came in. We must remember that we were going through a war period.

Here we are in 1973 and we're all very happy to redo some of these things and put them down as a matter of record. So now I just want to wish you the greatest. I'm going to miss you, old buddy, because when I don't check in with you once or twice 4 week -

You're not going to miss me because I'm going to get you fired like I always do and you probably will have to come over to join Milt Buckner and myself, because we did that with Slam Stewart and I'm pretty sure that with the friends that we know out here, we can get you fired and have you to come over to join us. (laughs)
I'll send for Slam any day, any week.

You just send for Milt Hinton. As a keynote, people do not know what it means to become a star. It is to become an individual, like a Fats Waller, like a Louis Armstrong, like a Dizzy Gillespie, like a Charlie Parker, like an Art Tatum, or like an Erroll Garner. It takes a long time to become an individual. The only way we get this, Milt, you know how it is - it's the way we live. You know it's very difficult. We would love to play with each other all the time, but circumstances do not warrant the fact that we can play with each other like in baseball or football. You would love to have the great football
JONES 216

player over here. Incidentally, Milt, I will tell you this now. I said it when they opened up a place when I was with the baseball players. I said, "Why don't you get a baseball player that can be to bat for the pitcher?" Now I'm the only person in the world that has ever said that they should have a baseball pitcher to bat instead of the pitcher batting -
Oh, a pinch hitter. *

Pinch hitter. Now they got to go controversial now. But what happens, music and sports and education is the only things that we've had the keyword in the whole world for 2,000, 3,000, 5-, 6,000 years. But we are fortunate that the musicians and sports is the two keywords to put the sweetening in the cake. You will notice that all athletes, he'll always try to play guitar, he'll try to play trumpet, he'll try to do everything. How do you think you're going to get a man like Stan Musial? The man liked guitar, but he's an athlete.
Rosey Grier.

I took him to Manny's to get him his guitar. I personally took him to Manny's, with Manny's son. But that is what we're talking about - we're dealing with human life now. Music and sports are the two major keys out here. It has always been when the peoples had wars years ago, 10,000 years ago, they got the musicians, they got the

*What became the "designated hitter" employed by the American league.
**Manny's Musical Instruments & Accessories, West 48th Street, Manhattan.
JONES
artists, you see. Now here we are in 1973.
There's the phone, Jo, hold it. In your own words, it's been mighty mice.

That's when Basie was going to the wrong dentist and he's on the network of CBS and it was very rare that a bandleader will ever speak from coast to coast. He was trying to say "mighty nice" and he said, "Don't you think it's mighty mice?" He said "mighty mice."

Oh, that's beautiful. Thank you, Jo. Hey Jo, I'd like to play a couple of tracks from your album here, the Jo Jones Plus Two on the Vanguard Studio Lab Jazz Showcase. I think the first track on here is "Satan Doll" and it shows the greatness of all of you guys with Jo Jones on drums, on here. The Jo Jones Trio/Featuring Tommy Bryant on bass and the great Ray Bryant on piano- two Philadelphia cats and a Chicago cat.
(MUSIC) (Second track is Bryant's "Little Suzie."

segments.title: Opening of the Hinton-Jones interview, New York, January 1973
segments.summary: Hinton introduces the NEA oral history session with drummer Jo Jones and greets him as his old section partner.

segments.title: Birth in Chicago and his father's travelling work
segments.summary: Jones gives his birth date (October 7, 1911), his parents' names, and says his father, a government artificer, was shifted around the country.

segments.title: The childhood burn that left him an invalid
segments.summary: He recalls burning himself copying an uncle lighting a cigar and being an invalid for a year and a half; his father brought him a ukulele.

segments.title: His sister Lillian
segments.summary: He names his one sister, Lillian, in New Jersey, and describes her career at Marshall Field's and as a dietician.

segments.title: Recovering from the affliction; family moving wherever father was called
segments.summary: Jones says he did not recover until about 16 or 17, was burned head to foot, and explains his father's skilled work took the family from place to place.

segments.title: His father's death in Tuscaloosa, 1922
segments.summary: He describes how his father died on July 17, 1922, struck by steel while helping black college students on a barge in Tuscaloosa.

segments.title: Aunt Mattie, Captain Baker and his father's shipbuilding in Alabama
segments.summary: Asked about early music interest, Jones introduces his aunt Mattie and recalls his father working for Captain Baker on the Warrior River and diving without a suit.

segments.title: Hearing Emil Helmicke's bass drum at the circus
segments.summary: Aunt Mattie took him to the Ringling Brothers circus where the bass drum of Emil Helmicke hit him in the stomach; she then bought him a drum.

segments.title: Jones wants to cover the unrecorded years 1926 to 1936
segments.summary: Jones mentions his unpublished writing and complains that histories begin with him joining Basie, skipping the years from 1926 to 1936.

segments.title: Phone calls from Earl Warren, Claude Hopkins, Roy Eldridge and Buddy Rich
segments.summary: The tape is stopped for phone calls from old friends, which both men call spiritual coincidences.

segments.title: First snare drum and people he met around Birmingham
segments.summary: Jones describes the snare drum his aunt bought and his Birmingham, Alabama neighborhood, naming people who shaped his life.

segments.title: Tuggle Institute, George Hudson and learning trumpet
segments.summary: He attended Tuggle Institute in Birmingham, a school for underprivileged children, where George Hudson taught him trumpet; schoolmates included Walter Young and Hunch Grimes.

segments.title: Edgar Battle and the Jack Hoxie show; study with James H. Wilson in Huntsville
segments.summary: Jones praises Edgar Battle as bandleader of Jack Hoxie's show, then describes studying at A and M in Huntsville with cornetist James H. Wilson.

segments.title: Wilson tells him about Louis Armstrong; he gives up trumpet and sax for piano
segments.summary: Mr. Wilson sends him to Louis Armstrong, whom he hears with Erskine Tate in Chicago; he abandons trumpet, sees Hawkins make sax hopeless, and moves to piano.

segments.title: On the road in 1930 with shows, doing everything, show-business discipline
segments.summary: In 1930 he plays drums, piano, sax, sings and dances with shows; he recalls show people's strict discipline and the Billboard blacklist.

segments.title: Black touring shows: Butterbeans and Suzie, Ida Cox, Ethel Waters
segments.summary: Jones recalls meeting Butterbeans and Suzie in Birmingham and describes the big black acts, Eddie Lemons, Ida Cox, and the record Hinton and he made with her.

segments.title: Erskine Hawkins, trumpet second parts and losing his embouchure
segments.summary: Jones says he played second trumpet parts until a prizefighter drummer, Kid Lips Hackett, led him to box, and his embouchure went.

segments.title: Adelaide Hall's three pianists in Omaha; pushing players off jobs
segments.summary: In Omaha around 1930 he hears Adelaide Hall with Art Tatum and Joe Turner and describes switching between piano and drums to take jobs.

segments.title: Manzie Campbell, Collier's Shows and the Eko and Iko act
segments.summary: He praises Manzie Campbell as the greatest drummer, who could roll perfectly with his left hand, and describes the sideshow of Collier's Shows.

segments.title: Crack Johnson, drummer in the Ringling tent
segments.summary: Jones describes Crack Johnson, an Oklahoma drummer resembling Jack Johnson, who played in the big tent with Sousa.

segments.title: Manzie Campbell's lesson and Collier Shows comedians
segments.summary: Years later, Campbell advised Jones not to repeat a mistake at the drums; Jones recalls Collier's Shows with Johnny Hudgins, Johnny Knox and Pigmeat.

segments.title: Not planning on music; Switzerland and pianist Calvin
segments.summary: Asked about dance bands, Jones says he intended to be a surgeon and go to Switzerland at 16 until his mother said he could not go unless Calvin did.

segments.title: Playing in white roadhouse bands before learning about color
segments.summary: When shows got stranded he sat in with white roadhouse bands and says he did not learn about colored and white until 19 or 20.

segments.title: Carnival people's training and the early hotel problem for musicians
segments.summary: Carnival performers taught the young musicians hygiene and discipline; he says musicians and ballplayers were turned away from hotels because of their trade.

segments.title: Omaha bandleaders required married men; Holland Harold
segments.summary: Leaders in Omaha refused unmarried musicians, so he ended up working with Holland Harold, who helped his musical education.

segments.title: His marriage to Vivian Greenne, 1933
segments.summary: He tells the comic story of marrying Vivian Greenne in Omaha on June 23, 1933, urged by Buddy Tate's wife Vi, with his mother visiting.

segments.title: Peacock Inn with Jimmy Jones's band, WOW radio and singing "All of Me"
segments.summary: Jones recalls 30 weeks at the Peacock Inn, pay with tips, letters from Kansas City friends, and singing hit tunes on WOW radio.

segments.title: Jesse Stone's band and Coleman Hawkins in Kansas City
segments.summary: He mentions Jesse Stone's 17-piece band and recalls that Coleman Hawkins's family required a guardian to travel with him.

segments.title: Kansas City wages compared with Omaha
segments.summary: Jones thought Kansas City musicians earned fortunes but Andy Kirk's men made $17.50 and Moten's $16.50, less than his Omaha job.

segments.title: Bennie Moten as the greatest bandleader
segments.summary: Jones calls Bennie Moten the greatest bandleader of all, the source of later styles, who came to New York first in 1930 with Jimmy Rushing.

segments.title: Walter Page's Blue Devils, Rushing and Basie moving to Moten
segments.summary: He describes Walter Page's Blue Devils, how Jimmy Rushing left first, then Basie, joining Bennie Moten.

segments.title: How Moten's and Page's rhythm sections joined to make Basie's rhythm section
segments.summary: Moten played one and three, Page two and four; together they made four, which Jones says is the root of Basie's rhythm section.

segments.title: Blue Devils drummers, Alvin Burroughs and George E. Lee's brass sections
segments.summary: He tries to recall the Blue Devils' drummer, says Alvin Burroughs went to George E. Lee, and praises the Midwest brass sections.

segments.title: Rushing joins Moten; drummer Mac Washington
segments.summary: Hinton sorts out the lineage; Jones describes Moten's drummer Mac Washington and his drop-in-the-bucket stumbles.

segments.title: Tips, the kitty and the $17.50 wage
segments.summary: Hinton asks about the slang for tips; Jones explains the kitty and splitting tips.

segments.title: Moten's New York visit and the battle of bands tours
segments.summary: Jones says Walter Page joined Moten in 1932 and describes five-band battle-of-bands tours with Chick Webb and others.

segments.title: Allen MacMillan and band tour coordination
segments.summary: Jones names Allen MacMillan as the man who coordinated tours, and Hinton identifies him as Louis Armstrong's publicist.

segments.title: Band contests: Edwards Collegians, Belton's Syncopators, Cannonball's father
segments.summary: He recalls yearly contests in Chicago and Detroit and Belton's Syncopators, where Cannonball Adderley's father played.

segments.title: Leaving Omaha: the ten-piece band with nine leaders
segments.summary: Jones describes a band in Omaha that changed leaders and uniforms at each gangster-run job, mentioning Elmer Crumley and Mary Osborne.

segments.title: Joining Tommy Douglas in Joplin, 1933
segments.summary: He came to Kansas City in 1933, replacing Jesse Price with Tommy Douglas's band in Joplin as drummer and singer.

segments.title: One night with Basie in Topeka; Lester Young's chorus on "After You've Gone"
segments.summary: Walter Page invites him to join Basie; after one night in Topeka, shaken by Lester Young's solo, he refuses pay and decides to return to school.

segments.title: Walter Page, Joe Keyes and Ben Webster try to keep him in the band
segments.summary: Page, Ben Webster and Joe Keyes pressure him to join Basie, but he insists he can only play five or six pieces.

segments.title: Fletcher Henderson's band in Kansas City, December 1933
segments.summary: He recalls Fletcher Henderson's band visiting with Coleman Hawkins, Bobby Stark and Dickie Wells, and going around with Stark.

segments.title: Hawkins hears Basie's band after hours; the buddha on the bandstand
segments.summary: After hours Henderson's men hear Basie's band with its rocking buddha, and Hawkins is challenged by the Kansas City saxophone players including Herschel Evans.

segments.title: Herschel Evans, Lester Young and Jack Washington
segments.summary: Jones calls Herschel Evans the greatest musician he played with, says Lester stayed in the band with difficulty afterward, and praises Jack Washington.

segments.title: Staying two weeks that became fourteen years with Basie
segments.summary: Returning for his drums, he is talked into staying; he told Basie he'd play two weeks until a drummer was found, and it lasted 14 years.

segments.title: Little Rock at Sam Baker's: short pay, a pawned bass drum and heating the head
segments.summary: At Sam Baker's in Little Rock he was paid $5 instead of $14 to cover the previous drummer's debt, and had to warm his bass drum by a stove.

segments.title: Personnel of the early Basie band of thirteen pieces
segments.summary: Jones lists the reeds, trumpets and trombone of the early band, including Lester Young, Buster Smith and Hot Lips Page, and Herschel and Lester's switching.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: Cliff McTyre, Freddie Green and Walter Page's rhythm guitar
segments.summary: He describes guitarist Cliff McTyre, how Freddie Green came into the rhythm section, and Page correcting how the guitar should play.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: Walter Page's many instruments and the bands Jones listened to
segments.summary: He recalls Page on baritone, tuba and bass, and says he heard Edwards Collegians, McKinney's and George E. Lee's band as a kid.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: Hinton asks what it felt like to be in the Basie rhythm section
segments.summary: Hinton praises the Basie rhythm section of Jones, Page, Green and Basie and asks what it was like inside it.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: "We lived spiritually": how the four-man section functioned
segments.summary: Jones says the four men brought their personal lives onto their instruments and played from a spiritual ingredient.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: Never hearing the band: playing as one
segments.summary: Jones says the section played with itself, gave each note its value and succeeded because of the lives they had lived together.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: Bennie and Bus Moten; Basie's debt to Moten
segments.summary: Jones recalls Bennie Moten sitting at the piano and settling the band, while Basie and Bus Moten were busy elsewhere.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: Hinton asks about Walter Page; Jones says nothing exists without him
segments.summary: Page is the one member of the section who has died, and Jones says without him no one would have heard of Rushing, Lester Young or Jo Jones.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: Refusing to leave Kansas City for New York without Walter Page
segments.summary: Jones recalls the band insisting Page come to New York, begging his wife, and turning down higher-paying offers from Cab Calloway and Claude Hopkins.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: His first wife on Cab Calloway's quiz show; the loss of their first child
segments.summary: He recalls his wife appearing on a quiz show and the death of their first child, a boy, in Omaha, before Joanne was born.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: What musicians' families sacrifice
segments.summary: Hinton and Jones talk about the toll of travel on musicians' wives and children and the unseen supports that sustained them.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: Neighbors, tradesmen and ward bosses who looked after musicians' families
segments.summary: Jones explains how cab drivers, shoeshine boys, pool-hall owners and political bosses looked in on families, and played tunes in return.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: His son born in 1937, the death of his first wife in 1946
segments.summary: Jones recalls staying in New York when his son was born on January 4, 1937, and Hinton recalls his wife's death in 1946 and how life shaped the section.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: Second marriage to Lorraine; becoming father and grandfather the same day
segments.summary: He discusses marrying Lorraine, their daughter Barbara, being a father and grandfather at once at the Embers, and his eight grandchildren.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: Start of the second set of tapes
segments.summary: After a silence, Hinton restarts the recording, noting the date and that they will play Jones's records.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: Blues guitarists converge on Paducah and the Decca rhythm section date
segments.summary: Jones describes recapitulating the blues for the Decca rhythm section recordings, and where guitarists and banjo players gathered in the South.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: Levee camps and the blues singers; a medicine show with Jim Jackson
segments.summary: He explains levee-camp entertainment for Tampa Red and others, and recalls taking over for Stepin Fetchit on a medicine show.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: The All-American Rhythm Section Decca session, about 1938
segments.summary: Hinton introduces their rhythm section records; Jones recalls recording on two mikes at Decca with Basie, Green and Page.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: Identifying the tracks: Pinetop Smith, Leroy Carr, Speckled Red
segments.summary: Hinton reads the track labels as music plays and Jones identifies the compositions and writers.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: Leroy Carr, the blues singer from Indianapolis
segments.summary: Jones describes Leroy Carr, who kept black artists in view in the early Depression, and compares him to Jelly Roll Morton.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: Song titles of the 1920s blues and their later recordings
segments.summary: Hinton and Jones discuss which tracks to play and how Black artists' songs were named after people and places in the 1920s.

segments.chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
segments.title: Playing the Kansas City Six sides; Freddie Green sings "Them There Eyes"
segments.summary: Hinton plays Commodore sides with Lester Young and the Kansas City Six, and Jones says Freddie Green sang "Them There Eyes" in 1937.

segments.title: Tape change and new session, January 23, 1973
segments.summary: Hinton turns the tape for a fresh subject and resumes two days after the last session.

segments.title: The Basie band of 1944 and its trumpet section
segments.summary: Jones says he stayed with Basie until September 1944 and names Joe Newman, Ed Lewis, Harry Edison and Al Killian at the Lincoln Hotel.

segments.title: Leaving for the Army; Shadow Wilson subs; Walter Page sent home
segments.summary: He left the Lincoln Hotel for the Army, with Shadow Wilson playing for a week, while Walter Page was sent home to settle family troubles.

segments.title: Basie's 1936 personnel: brass, reeds, Caughey Roberts, Claude Williams
segments.summary: Jones names the four brass and the saxophones of the band that came to New York in 1936, with Caughey Roberts replaced by Earl Warren, and Claude Williams on guitar and violin.

segments.title: The Billie Holiday date with Benny Goodman and Freddie Green joining
segments.summary: He recalls a January 1937 Billie Holiday recording with Goodman, Teddy Wilson and the Basie men, after which Freddie Green joined the band.

segments.title: Trumpet and trombone changes: Shad Collins, Harry Edison, Dickie Wells, Benny Morton
segments.summary: Jones traces who joined the brass in 1937-38 as the band grew to four trumpets and three trombones.

segments.title: Eddie Durham and the electric guitar
segments.summary: He praises Eddie Durham as the first to bring the electric guitar into focus, recalls his amplifier being stolen in Baltimore, and Benny Morton's arrival.

segments.title: Billie Holiday joins the band; moving up the theater circuit
segments.summary: Billie Holiday joined in 1937 as the band's first woman singer; Jones describes the progression from the Palace through the Apollo to the Paramount.

segments.title: Jimmy Rushing's change from ballads to blues
segments.summary: Jones explains that Rushing sang ballads until Decca and New York turned him into a blues singer.

segments.title: The battle against Chick Webb at the Savoy and the Carnegie Hall night
segments.summary: Jones recalls the January 1937 battle of music with Chick Webb, Ella and Billie, the same night as Goodman's Carnegie Hall concert, and Ellington at the Criterion.

segments.title: Touring with Billie Holiday and the crooked bus
segments.summary: Jones describes the one-nighters, the band's poor bus that was swapped for a good one near New York, so they looked like a big act.

segments.title: Billie Holiday wins the dice game; Lester Young's luck
segments.summary: He tells how Billie Holiday won everyone's money shooting dice on the bus and that Lester Young never won, then returns to the Chick Webb battle of January 1938.

segments.title: Nicknames and identities among musicians
segments.summary: Hinton and Jones talk about nicknames like Satchel Mouth and Mule Face and why musicians gave each other identities.

segments.title: How Billie became "Lady Day" and Lester became "Pres"
segments.summary: Jones says the name Lady Day began on a Baltimore bus when Lester mocked Jones's defense of a lady, and Billie named Lester Pres.

segments.title: Lester Young's birthplace and his love for the black race
segments.summary: Jones says Lester was born in Mississippi, loved the black race more than anyone, and that Jones looked after his affairs and buried him.

segments.title: Lester's speech, "Lady" and Pee Wee Marquette
segments.summary: Jones recalls Lester calling everyone Lady, his lucky 13, and his running joke tipping Pee Wee Marquette.

segments.title: Lester as peacemaker in fights with Jacquet, Eldridge and Scotty
segments.summary: Jones tells two stories of Lester stepping between fighting friends, including taking the punch at Clark Monroe's Uptown House.

segments.title: Lester's sensitivity and the rumors about his manner
segments.summary: Asked about rumors of effeminacy, Jones insists Lester was tender and hated seeing anyone mistreated.

segments.title: What the band called Lester; how "Lady Day" caught on
segments.summary: Jones says the band called him Lester while the world said Pres, and recounts how "Lady" and then "Lady Day" spread from the Uptown House.

segments.title: Billie Holiday leaves in early 1938; Basie's 1938 changes
segments.summary: Jones says Billie Holiday stayed nearly a year, leaving after the Chick Webb battle, and the band replaces its trumpets and trombones.

segments.title: Eddie Durham, Glenn Miller and "Slip Horn Jive" at the Famous Door
segments.summary: Jones says Eddie Durham took Basie arrangements to Glenn Miller's band, and Miller stopped visiting the Famous Door after Basie played "Slip Horn Jive" without music.

segments.title: California 1939 and the burning of the Pid-mor Ballroom
segments.summary: Jones describes the 1939 California trip and says a ballroom was burned down rather than let a black band play, then the Paramount and Treasure Island fair.

segments.title: When Lester Young left the band and Don Byas replaced him
segments.summary: They sort out the early 1940s, with Lester leaving for a USO tour with Al Sears and Don Byas taking his place.

segments.title: Bringing Lester back at the Lincoln Hotel
segments.summary: Basie sends Jones to find Lester on 52nd Street; Lester returns to the band without a word, and Jones notes he did not drink then.

segments.title: Glenn Miller's Navy Band offer; Lester and Jones drafted days apart
segments.summary: Jones turned down a Navy Band post arranged by Glenn Miller, and he and Lester entered the Army in 1944, days apart.

segments.title: How the Army treated Lester; "Break up Basie"; Jones as infantry soldier
segments.summary: Jones says the Army treated Lester Young shamefully and suggests an effort to break up Basie's band; he himself chose infantry and refused to play drums.

segments.title: Lester's treatment at Fort McClellan: the photo of his white wife
segments.summary: He says Lester was punished after a footlocker search found his wife was white, and Jones was made his guard; Ken Bluett is identified.

segments.title: Billy Goodall and Lester's treatment in Georgia
segments.summary: Jones recalls a bass player guarding Lester at gunpoint to make him play, and Lester's transfer to Camp Stewart.

segments.title: The trumpet-player MP who had to insult Lester for show
segments.summary: Jones describes a white trumpet player-turned-MP who had to insult Lester before black prisoners to keep up appearances.

segments.title: The same MP and the Fayetteville bus killing
segments.summary: Jones says the same MP later shot a bus driver who choked a black baby in North Carolina and was jailed at Fort Ord.

segments.chapter: Return to Basie and leaving in 1948
segments.title: Meeting Hinton and Cab Calloway at the Omaha Orpheum, February 1946
segments.summary: Fresh from the Army, Jones sat in with Cab Calloway's band in Omaha, replacing Shadow Wilson briefly and impressing Cab with Oliver Buford.

segments.chapter: Return to Basie and leaving in 1948
segments.title: Dannie Barker in Omaha and rejoining Basie in 1946
segments.summary: Jones tells how he introduced Dannie Barker to old circus musicians and then rejoined Basie in spring 1946.

segments.chapter: Return to Basie and leaving in 1948
segments.title: Lester Young at Camp Gordon, playing all day in the rec hall
segments.summary: Jones says Lester left the Army before him and was kept playing in the rec hall at Camp Gordon, put back in the prisoner area each night.

segments.chapter: Return to Basie and leaving in 1948
segments.title: Calling Basie from Fort Ord; "Cottage for Sale"; Norman Granz and Lester
segments.summary: From Fort Ord Jones telephoned Basie's band and Milt Ebbins, then visited Lester in Los Angeles, where Norman Granz began helping him.

segments.chapter: Return to Basie and leaving in 1948
segments.title: Declining Jazz at the Philharmonic; Illinois Jacquet in the Basie band
segments.summary: Jones stayed with Basie rather than join Granz's tour since Jacquet had already left, and recalls how Jacquet joined Basie.

segments.chapter: Return to Basie and leaving in 1948
segments.title: Recording "The King" in 1946 and the band's postwar personnel
segments.summary: Jones tells how he showed the band a groove on a sock cymbal for "The King," with Emmett Berry's solo and J. J. Johnson's last date.

segments.chapter: Return to Basie and leaving in 1948
segments.title: Basie's band personnel in 1946 and the one record he made before Omaha
segments.summary: Jones lists Jacquet, Buddy Tate, Preston Love and trombonists in the 1946 band, and explains he played just one record before leaving for Omaha.

segments.title: Cliff Leeman, a Kansas City drummer who went to New York
segments.summary: Hinton begins a survey of drummers; Jones says Cliff Leeman knew Kansas City music but could not transplant it to New York bands.

segments.title: Zutty Singleton and Baby Lovett
segments.summary: Jones says he missed Zutty on the circuit and calls Baby Lovett the best-looking drummer behind a set.

segments.title: Walter Bishop, Jimmy Bertrand and percussion in Chicago
segments.summary: Jones praises Walter Bishop and Jimmy Bertrand, who taught symphony players vibes, chimes and tympani, and again names Manzie Campbell.

segments.title: Alan Dawson and finding successors to teach
segments.summary: Hinton credits Alan Dawson with teaching Jones's sock cymbal and brush work; Jones recalls meeting him in Boston and sending him to a teacher.

segments.title: Kaiser Marshall, Walter Johnson, Sonny Greer and Ray McKinley
segments.summary: Jones compares Kaiser Marshall, Walter Johnson ("Mr. Drums"), Sonny Greer and Ray McKinley, favoring Johnson's finesse and McKinley's cleanness.

segments.title: Don Lamond and Sid Catlett at the Howard Theatre
segments.summary: Jones recalls Don Lamond and his girlfriend as the only white faces at the Howard Theatre, and how Sid Catlett brought him round.

segments.title: What segregation cost jazz between 1926 and 1936
segments.summary: Jones says musicians were kept from playing with whom they wished, and the music lost much because of social conditions.

segments.title: Gene Krupa upstairs
segments.summary: Jones recalls never meeting Gene Krupa because Krupa was always upstairs in the hotel when Jones played downstairs.

segments.title: Davy Tough crossing to the South Side
segments.summary: Jones credits Davy Tough with learning from Chicago's black musicians and showing white players what he heard.

segments.title: Tubby Hall and cabaret drummers; Chicago drummers
segments.summary: Jones calls Tubby Hall a cabaret drummer, saying only Jimmy Bertrand and Walter Bishop played the whole range.

segments.title: Lou Singer, Earl Palmer and Manzie Campbell
segments.summary: Jones tells how he introduced young drummers like Earl Palmer to Lou Singer and repeats that Manzie Campbell was the greatest he saw.

segments.title: Buddy Rich and drummers denied the chance to play with black bands
segments.summary: Jones says nobody knows drums like Buddy Rich but that he never had a Basie or Lunceford band to play with.

segments.title: Hinton's name game: Cliff Leeman, Ray McKinley, Gene Krupa
segments.summary: Hinton names drummers and Jones names their bands, including Leeman, McKinley and Krupa at Buddy Rogers's band.

segments.title: Davy Tough, George Wettling and the snare drum touch
segments.summary: Jones names George Wettling as better than Krupa and Tough and tells young drummers to listen to the snare drum touch of the greats.

segments.title: Sol Gubin; learning to tune drums from Jimmy Bertrand and Holland Harold
segments.summary: Jones says he learned drum tuning from Bertrand and from Holland Harold, an Omaha drummer and teacher.

segments.title: Cuba Austin and how Jones came to the high sock cymbal
segments.summary: He explains that he raised the sock cymbal on a pipe and a coat hanger out of necessity after seeing Cuba Austin's low model.

segments.title: Oliver Coleman, teacher
segments.summary: Jones praises Oliver Coleman, who taught more drummers than anyone, and recalls his last visit to him with cancer.

segments.title: Red Saunders, the Club DeLisa and Ike Day
segments.summary: Jones recalls Red Saunders bringing Lester to the Club DeLisa in 1936 and calls Ike Day one of the greatest drummers.

segments.title: Cozy Cole, Philly Joe Jones and Max Roach
segments.summary: Jones credits Cozy Cole as a teacher and speaks of Philly Joe and Max Roach, whom he knew when young.

segments.title: Jesse Price, Jimmy King, Freddie Jenkins; players who started on drums
segments.summary: Jones remembers Jesse Price, Jimmy King and Freddie Jenkins and notes that Roy Eldridge and Harry James began on drums.

segments.title: Sylvester Rice and Adolphus Osbrooke
segments.summary: Jones calls Sylvester Rice the best all-around drummer and conductor, who left New York disgusted for the Midwest.

segments.title: Jimmy Crawford, who urged him to come to New York
segments.summary: Jones praises Jimmy Crawford's sweetening of the Lunceford sound and says Crawford begged him to come to New York.

segments.title: Osie Johnson: bringing him to a record date and to New York
segments.summary: Hinton and Jones recall bringing young Osie Johnson to a Billy Williams record date and Jones's coaching of him in Washington and New York.

segments.title: Drummers trading jobs: J. C. Heard, Cozy Cole, Raymond Scott and Sid Catlett
segments.summary: Jones recounts how he steered J. C. Heard to Cab Calloway and Cozy Cole to Raymond Scott's CBS band, with Sid Catlett staying with Teddy Wilson.

segments.title: Jimmy Blanton's death and carrying Babs Gonzales to the doctor
segments.summary: Jones recalls Blanton's death around 1941 and carrying a collapsed Babs Gonzales to Doc Hawkins for hospital admission.

segments.title: Specs Powell, Sticks Evans and Billy Gladstone at Radio City
segments.summary: Jones tells how he kept Specs Powell in the drum chair and advised him and Sticks Evans to be percussionists, linking them to Radio City's Billy Gladstone.

segments.title: J. C. Heard joins Cab; Cozy Cole to CBS; Art Tatum at the Big Log
segments.summary: Hinton and Jones recall Cozy Cole's leaving Cab Calloway for CBS in 1943, and an evening in California with Art Tatum's trio.

segments.title: Cab Calloway's discipline and power
segments.summary: Jones praises Cab Calloway as a disciplinarian and, he says, the most powerful black man alive, who helped bands travel to Army camps in the war.

segments.title: Kansas Fields; the drum as the heartbeat and African origin of percussion
segments.summary: Jones talks of Kansas Fields, then says the drummer is the heart of the band, that the drum came from Africa, and what was lost by segregation.

segments.title: Kenny Clarke and bringing along the young drummers
segments.summary: Jones credits Kenny Clarke with Basie recordings credited to him and describes how veterans trained young drummers.

segments.title: O'Neil Spencer, John Kirby's drummer
segments.summary: Jones remembers O'Neil Spencer's drinking, knitting and playing with John Kirby.

segments.title: Kid Lips Hackett, showman drummer and prizefighter
segments.summary: Jones describes Kid Lips Hackett as a flipping, juggling showman who could also play symphony, and the act he planned with Sid Catlett.

segments.title: Lionel Hampton and the xylophone
segments.summary: Hinton adds Lionel Hampton; Jones says he got Hampton xylophones for speed and advised him to follow Red Norvo.

segments.title: What he did before Basie, and asking banjo and tuba men for help
segments.summary: Jones says he tried dancing, singing and drama before drums and learned from banjo, tuba and guitar players, who told him whom to look up.

segments.title: Ben Thigpen, his son Edmund, and Sonny Payne
segments.summary: Jones discusses Ben Thigpen and his drummer son, his own son's dancing, and tells Sonny Payne to learn touch from his father.

segments.title: Loss of the big bands and the missing farm system
segments.summary: Jones argues that after the war the dance floors and big bands vanished, leaving young players with no way to come up.

segments.title: Oliver Jackson and Eddie Locke; a break
segments.summary: Jones recalls mentoring two young drummers and telling them what to expect, before a short break.

segments.title: Chick Webb the epitome
segments.summary: After a break Jones praises Chick Webb's sense of timing and his several arrangements of one tune.

segments.title: Meeting Chick Webb in 1936 and learning his secrets
segments.summary: Jones recalls the summer of 1936, the Roseland opening, and Webb sharing tuning secrets and encouraging him.

segments.title: Chick Webb's encouragement: "be yourself"
segments.summary: Jones says Webb's advice to keep his naturalness and develop his own style kept him from leaving, and he taught him discipline.

segments.title: Another phone call from Buddy Rich
segments.summary: Hinton notes that another call interrupted, with Buddy Rich calling him the first time, and returns to Chick Webb.

segments.title: Webb's illness and wanting to join his band
segments.summary: Jones recalls Webb's kidney ailment and saying he nearly left Basie to learn from the dying bandleader.

segments.title: Phone interruption and a call from Bill Pemberton
segments.summary: The phone rings again, a call from Bill Pemberton, who helped Hinton tape Perry Bradford.

segments.title: Learning of Chick Webb's death in Chicago
segments.summary: Jones says friends hid the news of Webb's death for two days, and that Webb later appeared to him in a dream.

segments.title: Wanting to record excerpts of Chick Webb arrangements
segments.summary: Jones says he must record Chick Webb's arrangements such as "Harlem Carnival" and "Spanish Town" as a last crowning work.

segments.title: Hinton asks about John Hammond; Hammond arrives in Kansas City
segments.summary: Jones says Basie got letters from Charlie Barnet and John Hammond, and Hammond arrived at the black hotel in Kansas City in 1936.

segments.title: Hammond's challenge in Kansas City
segments.summary: Jones explains that Kansas City musicians were content at $17.50 and not interested in New York money, but Hammond had a flexibility that penetrated.

segments.title: First impressions of Hammond and the two letters
segments.summary: Jones tells Hammond he came to see Basie, not him, and says to answer Hammond's letter about bringing Basie to New York.

segments.title: Charlie Barnet's offer, Willard Alexander and Lester's praise of Billie Holiday
segments.summary: Jones describes Barnet's plan for Basie, Willard Alexander's visit to the Reno Club, and Lester telling him about Billie Holiday before Hammond.

segments.title: Willard Alexander, Milt Ebbins and Joe Glasser
segments.summary: Jones sorts out the managers and bookers around Basie, saying Alexander was the biggest in the business but did not know how to handle a black band.

segments.title: The Grand Terrace in Chicago, 1936
segments.summary: Jones recalls Basie fired at rehearsal at the Grand Terrace and kept on when Alma Turner defended them, playing for a month.

segments.title: Alma Turner defends the band to Ed Fox; Chicago radio broadcasts
segments.summary: Jones recalls the dancer Alma Turner cursing out Ed Fox over the bassoon parts so the band could play its own arrangements and take radio broadcasts.

segments.title: How John Hammond worked and why he is unrecognized
segments.summary: Jones describes Hammond starting many projects at once and setting up recording dates, and he and Hinton ask why the public does not know his role.

segments.title: John Hammond's contribution to jazz
segments.summary: After Bill Pemberton walks in, Jones calls Hammond the single force behind Granz, Wein, Gillespie and Charlie Parker's recognition, and Louis Armstrong's.

segments.chapter: Billie Holiday and the band's singers
segments.title: Billie Holiday joins Basie; the January 1937 record date
segments.summary: Jones explains why the band wanted a woman singer, and gives January 25, 1937 for the first Teddy Wilson date with Billie Holiday and the Basie men.

segments.chapter: Billie Holiday and the band's singers
segments.title: Bill Pemberton asks about the Teddy Wilson sessions
segments.summary: Pemberton asks about mixing men from different orchestras, and Jones says they were just trying to get a point across, not be commercial.

segments.chapter: Billie Holiday and the band's singers
segments.title: How the Teddy Wilson sessions drew on whichever band was in town
segments.summary: Hinton explains that the personnel came from the stars of whatever band was in New York, and Jones cites the January 30, 1939 session.

segments.chapter: Billie Holiday and the band's singers
segments.title: Helen Humes arrives; Hazel Scott and Rose Murphy at the Famous Door
segments.summary: After Billie stayed nearly a year, Helen Humes joined in July 1938, while Jones brought Hazel Scott in as intermission pianist.

segments.chapter: Billie Holiday and the band's singers
segments.title: Helen Humes, Thelma Carpenter and the band's women singers
segments.summary: Jones sorts out the sequence of women vocalists, from Billie to Helen Humes to Thelma Carpenter at the Lincoln Hotel's Blue Room.

segments.chapter: Billie Holiday and the band's singers
segments.title: Savannah Churchill and Baby Lawrence at the Regal in Chicago
segments.summary: Jones tells how the band, short of a woman on a theater bill, bought Savannah Churchill two dresses to sing "St. Louis Blues" and added dancer Baby Lawrence.

segments.chapter: Billie Holiday and the band's singers
segments.title: Thelma Carpenter: Coleman Hawkins, Kelly's Stable and Mother's Lunch in Boston
segments.summary: Jones describes the teenage Thelma Carpenter, returning her to the band, protecting her at Mrs. Fish's in Boston, and losing her to Eddie Cantor.

segments.chapter: Return to Basie and leaving in 1948
segments.title: Leaving Basie: back in March 1946, gone in 1948
segments.summary: Jones dates his Army service from September 1944, his return in March 1946, and his leaving Basie in 1948.

segments.chapter: Return to Basie and leaving in 1948
segments.title: Illness in 1948 and finding drummers to replace him
segments.summary: Jones says he left after his wife's death, stayed until Shadow Wilson and then J. C. Heard returned, and recommended Gus Johnson, who stayed to 1950.

segments.title: Birdland small group and Morris Levy's pay
segments.summary: Jones names Buddy DeFranco, Freddie Green and Joe Shulman in a Birdland group and says Morris Levy paid above union scale.

segments.title: The Teddy Wilson CBS show and album; resuming on January 29, 1973
segments.summary: Hinton plays a track from the Teddy Wilson, Jo Jones and Milt Hinton album from the CBS television show and resumes in the 1950s.

segments.title: The Embers: Jo Jones trio with Tyree Glenn and Hank Jones
segments.summary: They sort out the Embers jobs with Joe Bushkin, Tommy Potter and Hank Jones, and how his trio became Tyree Glenn's quartet for 17 and 16 weeks.

segments.title: The Jackie Gleason tour with Joe Bushkin and Buck Clayton
segments.summary: Jones and Hinton recall a five-to-six-week tour with Jackie Gleason's show and jazz stars, with a barbecue in Detroit and Gleason's generosity.

segments.title: The first Newport Jazz Festival
segments.summary: Jones recalls being house drummer at the first Newport festival in the rain, backing Billie Holiday with Hinton and Teddy Wilson.

segments.title: The Ray Bryant trio, San Juan, and the Jo Jones Plus Two album
segments.summary: Jones describes forming a trio with Ray and Tommy Bryant and then opening at Ochos Puertos in San Juan; Hinton praises the album.

segments.title: "Learn how to play with people, not for people"
segments.summary: Jones says the drummer must listen and play with people before playing for an audience, and that Walter Page and the bass taught him.

segments.title: Puerto Rican musicians: Escudero and Fernando Arbello
segments.summary: After a break Jones names the musicians he worked with in Puerto Rico.

segments.title: Garvin Bushell, who first took Coleman Hawkins out on the road
segments.summary: Hinton praises Garvin Bushell; Jones says he was Coleman Hawkins's guardian when Hawkins first left home, and that their mothers knew each other.

segments.title: Yearly trips to Europe with Milt Buckner and the tap dancers
segments.summary: Jones says he began going to Europe in 1969 with organist Milt Buckner and tap dancers Baby Lawrence and Jimmy Slide.

segments.title: The Panassie film made in France and Biarritz
segments.summary: They discuss the jazz film by Hugues Panassie's son, with Jones and Buckner on screen, and Jones's unplanned drum solo at Biarritz.

segments.title: The Duke Ellington Fellowship event at Yale, 1972
segments.summary: Hinton and Jones recall the Yale gathering with Eubie Blake, Duke Ellington, many drummers and bassists, and Jones asked to look after the elders.

segments.title: The bass choir and why the drummer needs the bass
segments.summary: Jones says he wanted a record with five bass players and that the foundation of the music is the tympani and the bass.

segments.title: Upcoming trip to Europe and a Harry Lim record date
segments.summary: Jones is about to leave for six weeks in Europe, and Hinton mentions an upcoming date with George Barnes produced by Harry Lim.

segments.title: Goodbyes between Hinton and Jones
segments.summary: Hinton says he will miss him and Jones jokes about getting him fired and sending for him in Europe.

segments.title: Becoming an individual; music and sports as keys
segments.summary: Jones says a star must become an individual, and that music and sports are the two keys to human life, with athletes who try to play instruments.

segments.title: Closing: Basie's "mighty mice" and playing tracks from Jo Jones Plus Two
segments.summary: Jones tells the story of Basie's slip on network radio, and Hinton plays tracks from the Jo Jones Plus Two album.
